QF.id: SIA Case Studies on SAS Standards_24

question.text: Under SAS-200, sanitation programmes can claim SROI. Which is the MOST commonly accepted monetary proxy for the OUTCOME 'averted diarrheal-disease burden'?

answer.text: Cost of treatment per diarrheal episode (WHO/public-health unit cost) × episodes averted, plus productivity-loss-day valuation
Average cost of bottled water per month
Cost of a toilet per household

explanation.text: The Logic: In SROI for sanitation/health programmes, monetary "proxies" are used to translate non-financial outcomes (such as diarrheal episodes averted) into rupee terms. The standard approach is to use established public-health unit costs: cost of treatment per diarrheal episode (drawn from WHO, ICMR or state public-health unit-cost data) multiplied by the number of episodes averted, plus a productivity-loss-per-day valuation (typically valued at minimum wage or per-capita income) for the avoided days of illness for the patient and caregiver. This proxy directly maps to the outcome being measured and is well-documented in social cost-benefit literature. The Trap: Average cost of bottled water per month is unrelated to disease burden and so is tangential. Cost of a toilet per household is an input/infrastructure cost, not a proxy for the health outcome of diarrhea averted. GDP per capita of India is a macroeconomic indicator far too coarse and aggregate to act as a per-episode monetary proxy. Only the treatment-cost-plus-productivity-loss combination matches the outcome being valued. Note: The cited workbook pages (59, 131, 151, 158, 161, 168-170 of the Social Impact Assessors Certification Examination Workbook) support SAS-200 health / sanitation case material and general SROI / monetisation concepts (requiring calculations, estimates, assumptions, and an audit trail), but they do not, in the pages checked, explicitly endorse the WHO diarrheal-episode treatment-cost plus productivity-loss proxy as written. The framing above reflects general public-health economics / SROI practice and standard social cost-benefit methodology.
